meta.title: The Note That Belongs to Both
meta.summary: Every neighbouring pair of CAGED windows shares one pentatonic note on every string, so a phrase can change window mid-stream on whatever string it already happens to be on.

spans.text: Positions in this pathway are written string, then fret —

means string 5, fret 3, and this lesson leans on that shorthand more than any before it. The windows overlap by design, so there are notes that belong to two of them at once, and a note like that is a doorway rather than a wall.

Chapter 3 found that on the low E string, each window's upper pentatonic dot is the next window's lower one. That turns out not to be a low-E-string curiosity. It is true on all six strings, in every neighbouring pair, with no exception — checked across all twenty-four cases, and every one of them hands over exactly one shared dot, on the string where the two windows meet.

That buys you something concrete. You do not have to get back to a particular string before you are allowed to change window. Whatever string a phrase happens to be on, there is a note under your hand that both windows own. Play it as the last note of the window you are leaving and the first note of the window you are entering, and nothing in the sound marks the change. The listener hears one phrase; you know it crossed a seam.
The easiest doorways to find are roots you already have — the same six positions chapter 1 spent a whole lesson counting.

The Root Ladder

Play the shared note as the last note of the window you are leaving and the first note of the window you are entering. Nothing in the sound has to mark the change, because the note does not know which window you think it belongs to.
Every root on the ladder you built starting in chapter 1 is a doorway of this kind, and

Along a String, Not Across the Neck
